QQQ paid about $1,500 on a $300,000 stake while VYM paid about $7,200, forcing QQQ holders to sell shares for living expenses.

NVIDIA and Apple sit atop QQQ, where size alone decides index membership and companies reinvest earnings in chips and data centers instead of paying dividends.

VYM beat QQQ on total return too, gaining about 14% versus 4% over one year, though growth funds have won other periods.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Consider a retiree with a hypothetical $300,000 in the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ). Over the past year, that position paid $1,524 in dividends. The same money in the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF (NYSEARCA:VYM) paid $7,164. If you count on a portfolio to pay for groceries and utilities, that gap decides how the money reaches you. Either it shows up on its own, or you have to sell shares to get it.

24/7 Wall St.
How Much Cash Each Fund Actually Paid

QQQ made four quarterly payouts with ex-dates (the cutoff for getting a dividend) from December 22, 2025 through September 21, 2026. Together, they came to $3.0918 per share. At its $608.45 price as of November 20, 2026, that works out to a trailing yield of 0.51%, or $1,524 on a hypothetical $300,000.

VYM's last four payouts, with ex-dates from December 19, 2025 through September 18, 2026, totaled $3.6755 per share. At its $153.92 price on November 20, 2026, that is a 2.39% trailing yield, or $7,164 on the same $300,000. These figures are the funds' past payments. They do not promise future income, and both will change as share prices move and as companies raise or cut their dividends.

Tony Dong

QQQ
QQQE

Quick Read

QQQ is highly concentrated: Its 10 largest holdings represented 46.46% of the portfolio as of November 11. QQQE instead equal-weights Nasdaq-100 constituents at approximately 1% each during quarterly rebalances.

Equal weighting is outperforming in 2026: As of November 13, QQQE had gained 13.17% year-to-date on a price-return basis, compared with 10.89% for QQQ, a 2.28% advantage.

Diversification comes with trade-offs: QQQE charges 0.35% versus QQQ's 0.18%, and quarterly rebalancing trims outperforming stocks, which can hurt during megacap-led rallies.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) has increasingly become a bet on the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, or bubble, depending on your perspective, continuing to grow. As of November 11, its 10 largest holdings accounted for 46.46% of the portfolio, with all seven Magnificent Seven stocks represented.

Wikimedia Commons

That's a considerable amount of concentration for an ETF holding 100 companies. While the Nasdaq-100 provides exposure to some of the world's most innovative businesses, its market-cap-weighted methodology means a relatively small number of trillion-dollar technology companies can have an outsized influence on returns. If those companies continue delivering strong earnings growth, that's great. But if AI spending disappoints or valuations contract, QQQ could face significant pressure even if many of its other holdings perform reasonably well.

Fortunately, investors who like the Nasdaq-100's methodology and constituent companies but don't want their fortunes tied to a handful of stocks have another option: the Direxion Nasdaq-100 Equal Weighted Index Shares (QQQE). It's one of Direxion's relatively few ETFs that don't use leveraged or inverse strategies, and I think it's particularly noteworthy today given the growing concerns surrounding concentration risk in the U.S. equity market.

Tech stocks fell hard on Friday, Nov 20. QQQ, a fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index, dropped 5.7% that day. Yet Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Exxon Mobil and Procter & Gamble all rose.

So did Johnson & Johnson win after past tech crashes? Mostly not. QQQ has had 13 falls of 20% or more since it began trading in March 1999. Johnson & Johnson held up better than QQQ in all 13. But in the year after the low, it beat QQQ only 6 times.

The middle result, called the median, shows the gap. In the year after a low, QQQ's median gain was 40.9% with dividends. Johnson & Johnson's was 13.9%. Holding up in a fall is not the same as winning the recovery.

Is this sell-off one of the past falls yet?

Procter & Gamble is up 14.1% since Oct 6, while QQQ is down 19.9%. If most of your savings sits in tech stocks, a drop that deep is hard to sleep through. Today's big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?

Update, Nov 23: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Nov 22, effective immediately. In Monday morning trading, SPY, a fund that tracks the S&P 500, rose about 5%, leaving it about 7% below its Oct 6 close. That is still below the Oct 6 high, so the bonds-first step below still applies, and the figures are at Friday's close.

The S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39 on Friday, Nov 20. That close was 11.6% below its Oct 6 high. A close 10% or more below a record closing high is called a correction. The Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ is down 19.9% from Oct 6. Gold did not help either. The gold fund GLD fell 15.5% over the same weeks.

You still have to sell something for next year's cash. Our answer is to sell the bond fund first, not the dividend fund. We ran a $2,000,000 portfolio through each correction our funds cover. Selling bonds first ended ahead of an even sale in 7 of 7 cases. Selling the dividend fund first ended ahead in none of them.

The test also found something bigger. How much you hold in stocks mattered more than which fund you sold. That was true in 7 of 7 cases.

How did we run the test?

The portfolio starts at $2,000,000 on the first close of each correction. It holds 40% in an S&P 500 fund, VOO. It holds 20% in a dividend fund, SCHD, and 40% in a bond fund, BND. Each year it pays out $80,000, which is 4% of the start. Dividends are reinvested. We measure the value five years later, or at the Nov 20 close when five years have not passed.

Selling the dividend fund first left the portfolio $24,068 behind an even sale on average. Selling bonds first left it $40,355 ahead on average.

Selling SCHD first during a correction left the portfolio $24,068 behind an even sale on average. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's. See how it held up.

We compared four ways to raise the $80,000. An even sale, called pro rata, takes a slice from each fund in line with its size. Bonds first takes the whole amount from BND while the S&P 500 stays below its old high. Dividend fund first does the same with SCHD. S&P 500 fund first does the same with VOO. The table below leaves that one out.

The 2007 case uses SPY and VYM, since VOO and SCHD did not exist yet. The 2022 and 2025 cases end at the Nov 20 close.

Shares of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) are up 31.1% at $164.57 as of 12:43 PM ET on Monday, Nov. 23. The catalyst is a leadership reversal. In a company announcement, NVIDIA said its board had reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board director. According to Barron's, the reinstatement followed direct intervention that President Donald Trump said was his own, and CNBC reported that Trump told the network, "I made the deal." NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

Take a hypothetical investor: a 66-year-old who moved $500,000 out of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:VOO) at Friday's close. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is up 4.33% from Friday's close as of 12:44 PM ET. On a $500,000 position, that works out to about $21,650 in a single session. Before today, the fund had fallen 4.37% over the past week, and a slide like that is exactly what tempts investors to step aside.

title: 4 ETF Winners of Last Week Amid Wall Street's Plunge
detail:
4 ETF Winners of Last Week Amid Wall Street's Plunge
Sanghamitra Saha
Mon, November 23, 2026 at 5:00 AM MST 3 min read
^GSPC
^DJI
^IXIC
^NDX

Wall Street was in the red last week, with the Nasdaq Composite losing as much as 10%, the S&P 500 retreating about 8.6%, the Dow Jones shedding about 8.1%. The S&P 500 and the Dow closed in correction while the Nasdaq 100 just had its worst week since March 2020.

Friday was the deadliest, with State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust SPY tumbling about 3.6% and Invesco QQQ Trust QQQ nosediving 5.7%. Fear gauge ETF ProShares VIX Short-Term Futures ETF VIXY jumped over 13% on Friday.

Inside the Slump

Wall Street's slump last week was driven by a combination of AI valuation concerns, renewed uncertainty over interest rates, profit-taking in technology stocks and weakening risk appetite.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq was particularly susceptible as investors reassessed whether massive AI spending would translate into earnings growth quickly enough to justify elevated valuations.

J.P. Morgan expects the Federal Reserve to deliver quarter-point rate hikes in January and March next year, ‌on top of a previously forecast December increase, as sticky inflation activates the need for further tightening, as quoted on Reuters.

Much-hyped Anthropic ANT IPO led investors to take profits on the rally rather than give Wall Street a reason to be in a strong upbeat momentum. ANT shares were down 15% last week. Meanwhile, NVIDIA NVDA saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking possible accounting issues at the company, per CNBC.  NVIDIA logged its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis.

ETF Winners

Against this backdrop, investors may want to know which ETF areas were steady last week. For them, below we highlight a few ETFs that survived the brutal week.

Cambria Tail Risk ETF TAIL – Up 9.7%

It is a tail-risk hedging ETF that generally holds Treasury securities and buys out-of-the-money S&P 500 put options. It protects portfolios against severe equity-market declines.

AGF US Market Neutral Anti Beta Fund BTAL – Up 3.6%

BTAL is designed to benefit when low-beta stocks outperform high-beta stocks. So, BTAL is surging recently due to a shift toward defensive, lower-volatility stocks relative to riskier, high-beta stocks.

iShares India 50 ETF INDY – Up 3.5%

Improving investor sentiment, foreign capital flows, a rebound in Indian equities after earlier weakness and a global chorus of anti-AI trade boosted Indian equities in recent days. Indian equities don't have significant exposure to the global semiconductor and AI supply chains – this very factor is mainly favoring the India trade.
